content.content: {"as_of":"2027-03-10T21:30:00-05:00","assignment_id":"engl-e2","from_version_id":"v3","to_version_id":"v4","paragraphs":[{"paragraph_id":"p1","change":"changed","from_text":"Last month the city council debated whether to make the 14 and 22 bus lines free for riders. Supporters packed the meeting, and so did a few business owners who were worried about the cost. This essay will look at both sides of the free-bus debate. I take the 22 to campus every morning, so I have seen who rides it and who does not. Most mornings the bus is full before it reaches the hospital stop.","to_text":"The city should make the 14 and 22 buses free for one year and count who rides. Last month the city council debated the idea, and supporters packed the meeting along with a few business owners worried about the cost. I take the 22 to campus every morning, so I have seen who rides it and who does not."},{"paragraph_id":"p2","change":"changed","from_text":"Fares are a bigger barrier than most people think, a monthly pass costs $64, which is more than many students spend on food in a week. A pass is cheaper per ride than single fares, but only if you can pay $64 at once. My roommate walks forty minutes to her job to save the fare, and some weeks she cannot afford the pass at all. When Riverton made its buses free two years ago, ridership went up. People who had stopped riding came back, especially older residents and part-time workers. Free fares would also save drivers the time they spend making change.","to_text":"Fares are a bigger barrier than most people think; a monthly pass costs $64, which is more than many students spend on food in a week. A pass is cheaper per ride than single fares, but only if you can pay $64 at once. My roommate walks forty minutes to her job to save the fare, and some weeks she cannot afford the pass at all. When Riverton made its buses free two years ago, ridership went up. People who had stopped riding came back, especially older residents and part-time workers. Free fares would also save drivers the time they spend making change."},{"paragraph_id":"p3","change":"changed","from_text":"The main objection is cost. Fares pay for about a fifth of the system, and the city would have to replace that money from somewhere. This is a fair point, and I understand why people worry about it. Some council members said a small fee keeps riders respectful, I do not think that is true. Most of the people I see on the 22 are tired, not rude.","to_text":"The main objection is cost. Fares pay for about a fifth of the system, and the city would have to replace that money from somewhere. This is a fair point, and I understand why people worry about it. Some council members said a small fee keeps riders respectful, but I do not think that is true. Most of the people I see on the 22 are tired, not rude."},{"paragraph_id":"p4","change":"unchanged","from_text":"Free buses would also help the environment. More riders means fewer cars downtown and less traffic near the hospital, where ambulances get stuck every afternoon. On my route I count at least ten cars for every bus at the Grant Street light. The council's own report says the downtown streets are already over capacity at rush hour. Cleaner air matters to everyone who lives near Grant Street. Buses would get crowded, but the city could add more.","to_text":"Free buses would also help the environment. More riders means fewer cars downtown and less traffic near the hospital, where ambulances get stuck every afternoon. On my route I count at least ten cars for every bus at the Grant Street light. The council's own report says the downtown streets are already over capacity at rush hour. Cleaner air matters to everyone who lives near Grant Street. Buses would get crowded, but the city could add more."},{"paragraph_id":"p5","change":"unchanged","from_text":"In conclusion, there are good arguments on both sides. Free buses cost money, but so do cars, parking and missed shifts. Students, nurses and part-time workers would feel the difference first. I think the city should try free buses on the 14 and 22 for one year and count who rides. If ridership grows the way it did in Riverton, the council will have its answer.","to_text":"In conclusion, there are good arguments on both sides. Free buses cost money, but so do cars, parking and missed shifts. Students, nurses and part-time workers would feel the difference first. I think the city should try free buses on the 14 and 22 for one year and count who rides. If ridership grows the way it did in Riverton, the council will have its answer."}],"status":"ok","app_id":"second-draft","version":{"epoch":2,"revision":4}}

paragraphs.from_text: Last month the city council debated whether to make the 14 and 22 bus lines free for riders. Supporters packed the meeting, and so did a few business owners who were worried about the cost. This essay will look at both sides of the free-bus debate. I take the 22 to campus every morning, so I have seen who rides it and who does not. Most mornings the bus is full before it reaches the hospital stop.
paragraphs.to_text: The city should make the 14 and 22 buses free for one year and count who rides. Last month the city council debated the idea, and supporters packed the meeting along with a few business owners worried about the cost. I take the 22 to campus every morning, so I have seen who rides it and who does not.

paragraphs.from_text: Fares are a bigger barrier than most people think, a monthly pass costs $64, which is more than many students spend on food in a week. A pass is cheaper per ride than single fares, but only if you can pay $64 at once. My roommate walks forty minutes to her job to save the fare, and some weeks she cannot afford the pass at all. When Riverton made its buses free two years ago, ridership went up. People who had stopped riding came back, especially older residents and part-time workers. Free fares would also save drivers the time they spend making change.

A pass is cheaper per ride than single fares, but only if you can pay $64 at once. My roommate walks forty minutes to her job to save the fare, and some weeks she cannot afford the pass at all. When Riverton made its buses free two years ago, ridership went up. People who had stopped riding came back, especially older residents and part-time workers. Free fares would also save drivers the time they spend making change.

paragraphs.from_text: The main objection is cost. Fares pay for about a fifth of the system, and the city would have to replace that money from somewhere. This is a fair point, and I understand why people worry about it. Some council members said a small fee keeps riders respectful, I do not think that is true. Most of the people I see on the 22 are tired, not rude.

Most of the people I see on the 22 are tired, not rude.

paragraphs.from_text: Free buses would also help the environment. More riders means fewer cars downtown and less traffic near the hospital, where ambulances get stuck every afternoon. On my route I count at least ten cars for every bus at the Grant Street light. The council's own report says the downtown streets are already over capacity at rush hour. Cleaner air matters to everyone who lives near Grant Street. Buses would get crowded, but the city could add more.

paragraphs.from_text: In conclusion, there are good arguments on both sides. Free buses cost money, but so do cars, parking and missed shifts. If ridership grows the way it did in Riverton, the council will have its answer.
